title: A Non-Freaked Out, Focused Approach to the Common Core — Part 2 — Complex Texts
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart lays out how he meets the Common Core's text-complexity shift by having whole classes read shared, extended, grade-level complex texts rather than relying mainly on 'just right' choice books. He credits Rafe Esquith, Mike Schmoker and colleague Doug Stark for the high-expectations approach, and lists the novels and articles his rural, high-poverty ninth graders read in ELA and world history. Confronting the strongest objection, that most students simply won't read assigned complex texts, he started tracking the daily percentage of students who completed the reading against a 70% 'win threshold'. He then details the moves that raised completion: a strong hook with key concept vocabulary, short early assignments with close reading of hard passages, quick comprehension checks, modeled reading, simple homework, question-driven discussion, in-class reading time with page checks, parent contact and repeated 'motivational speeches' about grit. He contrasts his approach respectfully with Penny Kittle's choice-plus-short-texts model, insisting there is no silver bullet, and closes with how complex texts serve as 'fenceposts' in his history course.
points: Stuart publicly tracks the class's daily reading-completion percentage against a 70% target, turning the common objection that students won't read hard books into a measurable problem he can work on.

His remedy is structural, not exhortation alone: start with 10-15 page assignments, closely read the hardest early passages, check basic comprehension at the top of each class and give 20-30 minutes of in-class reading while he checks pages.

He frames high expectations as respect, telling students that a society expecting little of them should make them angry and that difficult reading builds the delayed-gratification muscle successful people share.
He treats his whole-class approach and Penny Kittle's choice-reading model as trade-offs each teacher must weigh, since each pushes some students further and fails others.
In history, extended complex texts and articles serve as the deep 'fenceposts' on a chronological 'fence' built through textbook, videos and lecture.
quotes: If you've been hearing “complex text” phraseology thrown around like crazy lately, it's because one of the central shifts that the Common Core promotes is the idea that, instead of only giving students books that are within their zone of proximal development (“just right” books), we should be asking students to read texts that are appropriately complex for their age.

The most common (and powerful) critique of the extended whole-class text approach that I'm using is this: most students just won't (or just can't) read grade-level complex texts on their own. Therefore, it's a huge waste of time to assign anything more than an article-length complex text.

So, keeping that 46% in mind, I currently consider 70% the “win threshold.” As you can see above, Things Fall Apart — the first book I tracked — was pretty much a fail. However, we saw quite an increase in completion with our next extended complex text, All Quiet on the Western Front. If we can keep those numbers up during the remaining months of school, I'll be pumped. And I know that, even if students didn't finish the assigned reading, due to the way I've structured class, all are reading, writing about, and discussing large portions of it.

Start slow: More than once, I've felt pressure to cover a book quickly, and that pressure has led me to assign just as many pages at the beginning of a reading unit as I do at the end. This doesn't work well; many students quit.

And indeed, if it's true that most students won't read what's assigned, it is a wasted assignment for most students. So, seeking to determine what percentage of my students were reading the assigned texts, I began tracking the percentage who had completed the previous day's reading assignment (see image below).

While I do use choice reading (most heavily in the first trimester), I don't choose to go “all in” on it. When I asked Penny for her reasoning in doing so, she honestly answered that she tries to weigh out what is gained and what is lost. I couldn't agree with her more in that kind of thinking; there is no “silver bullet” in education.

My goal as a world history teacher is to build a fence in my student's brains. The fence itself represents a chronological framework of world history; the fenceposts represent deeper learning experiences (e.g., digging into some source documents or articles; simulating socialism and capitalism; reading Escape from Camp 14 or Julius Caesar).
